title: Don't Tempt Me
full_review:
Heaven and hell battle for the soul of a washed-up boxer in the curious Spanish satire "Don't Tempt Me" (First Look).
The film from director Agustin Diaz Yanes had the potential to generate some interesting discussions on the mysteries of life after death while entertaining audiences with its wit. But the few thought-provoking ideas the film manages to put forth are drowned by the muddled and often banal ones, and it comes up short on the comedy side as well.

However, this is not to say that the film doesn't have some merit. Diaz Yanes creatively portrays heaven in delicious sepia tones as a 1930s nightclub in Paris. Hell is depicted as a backstabbing corporation where the management is -- not surprisingly -- only interested in climbing the corporate ladder without regard to who falls off the rungs.

The superb cast is likely to please fans of foreign films both for their appearance and their fine performances. French treasure Fanny Ardant is Marina D'Angelo, the sophisticated and charming director of operations for heaven. Her counterpart down under is Jack Davenport (Gael Garcia Bernal), chief executive of hell, a playboy with slick clothing and a stretch limo. Along with being the nightclub's star chanteuse, Lola Nevado (Victoria Abril) is also one of heaven's key angel operatives. Penelope Cruz stars as Carmen Ramos, a feisty waitress working in the 22nd circle of hell whose spunk lands her the job as Lola's foil.

The gist of the story is this: Souls are the commodity for which heaven and hell fiercely compete. Heaven is on the verge of bankruptcy when it gets a request from a mother to save her strong-willed son, Manny (Demian Bichir), a boxer who has had one too many blows to the head and is suffering from brain damage. But hell wants him, too. So Lola appears as Manny's wife, back to reunite with him, and Carmen shows up as his long-lost cousin, all grown up and needing a place to crash.

The film throws in a twist in Cruz's character, who was a male gangster here on Earth and has received the punishment of being turned into a woman who must wait on piggish men who harass her and treat her like dirt. This explains Carmen's attraction to women.

In its most simplistic form, "Don't Tempt Me" can be seen as presenting humans as merely pawns over which heaven and hell battle, like some Greek gods playing a game. It also resorts to having angel Lola do something "bad" in order to save Manny's soul. However, the film does get across the notion that even one soul is worth the effort, especially from heaven's point of view.
Yet the film contradicts itself several times, until it all becomes a confused mess that fails to convey any coherent message, maintain its initial quirky tone or engage the audience. And that's the basic problem with the film: It simply doesn't come together.

Subtitles.

Because of an implied sexual encounter and several sexual references, some harsh violence, much rough language and some profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
